title: A Stack That Knows Its Minimum

concept.title: Store the minimum next to every value
body: You want a stack with four operations that are all fast: `push`, `pop`, `top` and **`min`** (the smallest value currently in the stack). Looking for the minimum in the whole stack would cost O(n). The trick: when you push a value, also store **the smallest value of the stack at that moment**, i.e. the minimum of the new value and the minimum stored with the previous top.

body.code:
stack = []                      # pairs (value, minimum of this value and everything below)
push x:  stack.append((x, min(x, stack[-1][1]) if stack else x))
pop:     stack.pop()
top:     stack[-1][0]
min:     stack[-1][1]

body: Because the minimum is stored together with each value, it comes back automatically after a `pop`: the new top still carries the minimum of everything below it. All four operations take O(1).

statement: Process `n` operations on an initially empty stack. `push x` puts the number `x` on top. `pop` removes the top. `top` asks for the value on top. `min` asks for the smallest value in the stack. Every operation line has two words: the operation and a number; for `pop`, `top` and `min` the number is 0 and must be ignored. All operations are valid (the stack is not empty when `pop`, `top` or `min` is used). Print the answer of every `top` and `min` operation, one per line.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has an operation and a number.
outputFormat: One line for every `top` and `min` operation, in order.
constraints: There is at least one `top` or `min` operation.

examples.input:
7
push 5
push 2
push 8
min 0
pop 0
pop 0
top 0
examples.note: The minimum is 2; after two pops the top is 5.

hints: Store the minimum together with each value on the stack.
The new minimum is the smaller of `x` and the minimum stored with the current top.
After `pop`, the new top already knows the right minimum.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: Every stack entry stores the value and the minimum of the stack up to and including it, so `min` and `top` are constant-time reads of the top entry and `pop` restores the previous minimum automatically.
solution.complexity: Time O(1) per operation, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

stack = []
out = []
for op, val in ops:
    if op == "push":
        x = int(val)
        stack.append((x, min(x, stack[-1][1]) if stack else x))
    elif op == "pop":
        stack.pop()
    elif op == "top":
        out.append(stack[-1][0])
    else:
        out.append(stack[-1][1])
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))
